title: Practice Team Improvisation to Improve Execution
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article argues that skilled execution depends as much on improvisation as on the original plan, yet most teams only rehearse the plan and rarely practice adapting when things go wrong. It frames improvisation as a trainable skill built on two foundations: knowledge of the conventional playbook and a brainstormed sense of the possible adaptations available when circumstances shift. The piece recommends that after teams finish planning and rehearsing, leaders should deliberately walk through likely surprise scenarios and talk through how the team would respond. The core claim is that teams who have discussed a wide 'palette' of possible responses in advance are far more prepared to improvise smoothly when the unexpected inevitably happens.
points: Skilled execution relies as much on improvisation as on the original plan.
Teams commonly rehearse the plan itself but rarely practice adapting to surprises.
Improvisation rests on two foundations: knowing standard actions and having brainstormed possible adaptations.
Leaders should brainstorm likely unexpected scenarios with the team before execution, not just after problems arise.
Teams that know their 'palette' of possible responses can improvise smoothly under pressure.
quotes: Leaders and team members who execute skillfully are typically the best improvisers.
The ability to think creatively and develop workable solutions on the fly is the essential skill when executing.
Improvisation is not some arcane talent possessed only by great comedians.
Knowing those colors through team discussion and brainstorming is how great leaders prepare a team for flawless execution.
If plans are made with good intentions, execution is forged through creative preparation.
